plan.title: Vintage-Style Painted End Table
plan.summary: Build a compact end table inspired by the antique white table in the photo: a softly rounded top, four square legs, and shallow arched aprons. The photo does not show the whole table, so this plan uses a practical, sturdy size and recreates the vintage look with a distressed painted finish rather than carved details.
assumptions: The furniture to recreate is the end table visible beneath the vase, not the flower arrangement.
The table is estimated at 600 mm wide, 450 mm deep, and 650 mm high because no target size or reliable scale reference is provided.
Use 18 mm birch plywood for the top and straight, clear pine for the legs and aprons. The design substitutes straight legs and a simple arched apron for the photo's more ornate carved details.
The table is intended to hold ordinary household items, not people or unusually heavy loads.
The plywood top is stable across its width; metal angle brackets connect it to the frame without relying on glue across solid-wood grain.

parts.name: Rounded tabletop
parts.notes: Round the four corners to a 20 mm radius and ease the exposed edges.

parts.name: Straight table leg
parts.material: Clear pine, actual 45 x 45 mm stock
parts.notes: Cut all four legs to the same length; square ends keep the table level.

parts.name: Front and rear arched apron
parts.notes: The lower edge has a shallow, raised-center arch for a restrained vintage detail.

parts.name: Left and right arched apron
parts.notes: These side aprons fit between the front and rear legs. They meet the legs at their end faces; they do not overlap the front and rear aprons.

fasteners.name: Coarse-thread pocket-hole screws
fasteners.size: 32 mm; use the length specified by the jig manufacturer for 19 mm stock

joints.drive_from: From the inside face of each P3 apron end into the side-grain face of P2; drill pocket holes before assembly.
joints.note: Each front or rear apron connects to two legs. Use glue and two pocket screws per connection; do not drive into leg end grain. Test one joint first to verify screw length and that no tip protrudes.

fasteners.name: Coarse-thread pocket-hole screws
fasteners.size: 32 mm; use the length specified by the jig manufacturer for 19 mm stock

joints.drive_from: From the inside face of each P4 apron end into the side-grain face of P2; drill pocket holes before assembly.
joints.note: Each side apron connects to a front and rear leg. Use glue and two pocket screws per connection; do not drive into leg end grain. Test one joint first to verify screw length and that no tip protrudes.

joints.drive_from: Attach each bracket to the inside face of P3 before placing P1; then drive the remaining screws upward from below into the tabletop underside.
joints.note: Two brackets support each front or rear apron. Use two screws into the apron and two into the plywood top per bracket; do not glue the top to the frame.

joints.drive_from: Attach each bracket to the inside face of P4 before placing P1; then drive the remaining screws upward from below into the tabletop underside.
joints.note: Two brackets support each side apron. Use two screws into the apron and two into the plywood top per bracket; do not glue the top to the frame.

joints.drive_from: Attach each bracket to the inside face of a leg before placing P1; then drive the remaining screws upward from below into the tabletop underside.
joints.note: One bracket per leg connects the plywood top to the frame. Use short screws so none pierce the tabletop.

hardware.name: Coarse-thread pocket-hole screws
hardware.size: 32 mm, or the jig manufacturer's specified length for 19 mm stock
hardware.notes: Two per apron-to-leg connection. Test a sample joint first and confirm the screw tip does not protrude.

hardware.name: 25 x 25 mm steel angle brackets
hardware.notes: Four front/rear apron-to-top brackets, four side-apron-to-top brackets, and four leg-to-top brackets.

hardware.name: #8 pan-head screws
hardware.notes: Four per angle bracket: two attach the bracket to the frame and two attach it to the tabletop.

hardware.name: Wood glue
hardware.notes: One small bottle is sufficient for the structural apron-to-leg joints.

hardware.name: Pocket-hole jig
hardware.notes: Use the jig manufacturer's matching coarse-thread screw length; typically 32 mm for 19 mm stock.

finishes.name: Interior/exterior furniture primer
finishes.notes: Use a primer compatible with the chosen water-based furniture paint.

finishes.name: Water-based furniture paint, warm antique white
finishes.notes: Apply thin coats; lightly sand select edges between coats for a gently worn look.

finishes.name: Water-based clear satin topcoat
finishes.notes: Protects the tabletop and painted finish; follow the label for recoat and cure times.

tools.name: Tape measure, pencil, and combination square
Miter saw or circular saw with a straightedge
tools.alternative: Have a home center make the square cuts, or use a handsaw with a clamped guide.

tools.name: Jigsaw
tools.alternative: Have the apron profiles cut at a shop, or use a coping saw and sand the curves smooth.

tools.name: Pocket-hole jig and drill/driver
tools.alternative: A drill with a pocket-hole jig is needed for this joint method; a shop can drill the pocket holes if you do not own a jig.

tools.name: Clamps
tools.alternative: Use temporary strap clamps or ask a helper to hold the frame square while fastening.

tools.name: Random-orbit sander and sanding block
tools.alternative: Use sanding blocks and hand sanding; it takes longer but works well on this small project.

tools.name: Countersink/pilot bit and small drill bit
tools.alternative: Use a hand drill and a separate countersink bit.

tools.name: Paint brushes or small foam rollers

steps.title: Measure and cut the stock
steps.text: Cut P2 (legs), P3 (front and rear aprons), and P4 (side aprons) to their listed lengths. Cut P1 (top) to 600 x 450 mm if it is not already sized; mark 20 mm corner radii. Check every matching pair against one another before moving on.
tools_used: Tape measure, pencil, and combination square
Miter saw or circular saw with a straightedge
steps.safety: Wear eye and hearing protection when using a saw. Support sheet goods securely and keep hands clear of the blade.
steps.tip: Label the inside face of each apron and the four leg positions to make assembly easier.

steps.title: Shape the top and apron curves
steps.text: Round P1's corners to the marked 20 mm radius. Cut the shallow arched lower profiles in P3 and P4, keeping the top edges straight. Sand the cut edges smooth without changing the fit dimensions.
steps.safety: Clamp each piece before cutting; wear eye protection and keep the jigsaw cord clear of the blade.
steps.tip: Cut just outside the marked curve, then sand to the line for a smooth, even profile.

steps.title: Sand and drill the pocket holes
steps.text: Sand all parts through 120- then 180-grit, easing sharp edges. Drill two pocket holes near each end on the inside face of every P3 and P4 apron, following the jig setting for 19 mm stock. Make a test joint with the jig manufacturer's specified coarse-thread screw, typically 32 mm, and confirm the tip does not protrude before drilling the rest.
steps.safety: Wear a dust mask and eye protection while sanding and drilling; clamp work securely before drilling.
steps.tip: Do not put pocket holes in the visible outside faces of the aprons.

steps.title: Assemble the leg-and-apron frame
steps.text: Dry-fit the four legs and four aprons on a flat surface, with the aprons' top edges flush with the leg tops. Apply glue at each apron-to-leg contact. Drive two 32 mm pocket-hole screws per connection, or the jig manufacturer's specified length for 19 mm stock, from the inside apron faces into the side grain of the legs; check the frame for square before the glue sets.
steps.safety: Wear eye protection when driving screws and wipe up glue promptly to avoid a slippery floor.
steps.tip: Measure both frame diagonals; adjust the clamps until the measurements match.

steps.title: Attach the tabletop and support brackets
steps.text: With the frame upright, fasten two 25 x 25 mm angle brackets to each apron and one to each leg, keeping them below the frame's top edge. Use two 16 mm #8 screws into the frame for each bracket. Set P1 on the frame with its edges aligned to the frame's outside dimensions, then drive two 16 mm #8 screws upward through each bracket into the tabletop underside; do not add glue.
steps.safety: Use a helper to lift and position the top; wear eye protection while drilling and fastening from underneath.
steps.tip: Check that the tabletop corners align with the legs before fastening; keep the short screws from breaking through the top.

steps.title: Prime, paint, and distress lightly
steps.text: Fill visible dents, then remove dust with a clean cloth. Apply primer and let it dry as directed; apply two thin coats of warm antique-white furniture paint. For a gently aged look like the photo, lightly sand a few edges after the paint dries, stopping as soon as the primer shows.
tools_used: Paint brushes or small foam rollers
steps.safety: Work with ventilation, wear a suitable dust mask while sanding, and follow the paint label for handling and drying.
steps.tip: Test the distressing on an underside edge first; heavy sanding can make the finish look artificially damaged.

steps.title: Apply the protective finish and inspect
steps.text: Apply a thin water-based satin clear coat to the tabletop and painted surfaces, following the label for recoat time. Let the finish cure fully before placing objects on the table. Set the table on a level floor and check for rocking; correct any uneven leg with careful sanding.
tools_used: Paint brushes or small foam rollers
steps.safety: Ventilate the room and avoid flames or sparks around wet finish; follow the product label for protective equipment and drying times.
steps.tip: A felt pad on each foot can protect the floor, but use equal-thickness pads to keep the table level.

safety_overview: Wear safety glasses when cutting, drilling, and fastening; use hearing protection for powered saws.
Control wood dust with a dust mask and vacuum or outdoor sanding, especially during extended sanding.
Clamp stock before cutting or drilling, and keep hands outside the blade path.
Use paint and clear coat with good ventilation; follow each product label for PPE, recoat times, and full cure time.
Lift the tabletop with a helper if needed, and keep the work area clear of offcuts and cords.
